Course Code: GST 111
Course Title: Communication in English
Level: 100 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Effective communication in English, grammatical structure, reading comprehension, study skills, phonetics, sentence construction, note-taking, and academic essay composition.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Study skills, active listening and note-taking techniques.
Unit 2: Grammatical structures, sentence types, clauses, and concord.
Unit 3: Phonetics, phonology, and accurate pronunciation.
Unit 4: Reading comprehension and vocabulary expansion.
Unit 5: Academic paragraph and formal essay development.

Course Code: NAU GST 113
Course Title: Humanities
Level: 100 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Introduction to humanities, cultural heritage, social institutions, philosophy, arts, literature, ethics, and human values in contemporary African society.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: The concept, nature, and branches of humanities.
Unit 2: African traditional civilization and colonial impact.
Unit 3: Philosophy, moral ethics, and social justice.
Unit 4: Arts, music, and literary expressions in Nigeria.
Unit 5: Contemporary globalization, cultural preservation, and national identity.

Course Code: COS 101
Course Title: Introduction to Computer Science
Level: 100 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Foundations of computer systems, computer hardware architecture, system software, binary and hexadecimal arithmetic, problem-solving algorithms, flowcharts, and operating system concepts.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: History and generational evolution of computers.
Unit 2: Hardware architecture: CPU, memory, I/O devices, and storage.
Unit 3: Number systems: binary, octal, decimal, and hexadecimal conversions.
Unit 4: Logic gates and Boolean representation.
Unit 5: Algorithm design, pseudocode, flowchart conventions, and intro to programming.

Course Code: MTH 101
Course Title: Elementary Mathematics I
Level: 100 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Elementary set theory, subsets, operations on sets, Venn diagrams, real number system, indices, surds, logarithms, quadratic equations, progressions (AP & GP), and mathematical induction.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Set theory: union, intersection, complement, Cartesian products, and Venn diagrams.
Unit 2: Real number axioms, inequalities, and absolute values.
Unit 3: Indices, logarithms, surds, and radical equations.
Unit 4: Theory of quadratic equations, roots, and polynomial factorization.
Unit 5: Arithmetic and Geometric Progressions, binomial theorem, and induction.

Course Code: STA 111
Course Title: Descriptive Statistics
Level: 100 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Definition, nature, and scope of statistics. Methods of data collection, classification, tabulation, frequency distributions, graphical representation, measures of central tendency, dispersion, skewness, and kurtosis.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Nature of statistical inquiry, primary and secondary data collection.
Unit 2: Frequency distribution tables, histograms, ogives, frequency polygons, and pie charts.
Unit 3: Measures of central tendency: Mean (arithmetic, geometric, harmonic), Median, Mode, Quantiles.
Unit 4: Measures of dispersion: Range, Mean Deviation, Variance, Standard Deviation, and Quartile Deviation.
Unit 5: Moments, Pearsonian and Bowley measures of Skewness and Kurtosis.

Course Code: STA 121
Course Title: Statistical Inference I
Level: 100 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Basic concepts of statistical inference, populations, random sampling, introduction to probability concepts, point and interval estimation for large samples, and elementary formulation of hypothesis testing.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Population and sample definitions, parameter vs statistic.
Unit 2: Random sampling techniques and sampling distributions.
Unit 3: Point estimation concepts: unbiasedness, consistency, and standard errors.
Unit 4: Confidence interval construction for population mean and proportion.
Unit 5: Introduction to statistical hypotheses: Null, Alternative, Type I & II errors, and Z-tests.

Course Code: NAU-PHY101
Course Title: General Physics I
Level: 100 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Mechanics, thermal physics, properties of matter, dimensional analysis, rectilinear motion, Newton's laws of motion, work, energy, power, rotational dynamics, elasticity, and fluids.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Units, physical dimensions, and dimensional analysis.
Unit 2: Kinematics: vectors, projectiles, velocity, and acceleration.
Unit 3: Newton's laws, friction, momentum conservation, and collisions.
Unit 4: Circular motion, gravitation, work, power, and kinetic/potential energy.
Unit 5: Hydrostatics, Archimedes' principle, surface tension, viscosity, and thermal expansion.

Course Code: NAU-BIO 101
Course Title: General Biology
Level: 100 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Fundamental biological principles, ultrastructure of living cells, cellular reproduction, mitosis, meiosis, Mendelian genetics, diversity of living organisms, ecology, and energy flow in ecosystems.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Chemical basis of life, macromolecule structure and biological enzymes.
Unit 2: Cellular anatomy: prokaryotic vs eukaryotic organelles and membrane transport.
Unit 3: Cell division: mitosis, meiosis, and gametogenesis.
Unit 4: Classical Mendelian genetics, monohybrid/dihybrid crosses, and sex linkage.
Unit 5: Principles of ecology, ecosystems, trophic pyramids, and environmental conservation.

Course Code: ECO 111
Course Title: Principles of Economics
Level: 100 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Fundamental concepts of microeconomics, scarcity, choice, scale of preference, opportunity cost, laws of demand and supply, elasticity, consumer behavior, and price mechanisms.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Basic economic problems: scarcity, choice, opportunity cost, and production possibility curves.
Unit 2: Demand theory: determinants, demand function, and law of demand.
Unit 3: Supply theory: determinants, supply elasticity, and market equilibrium.
Unit 4: Price elasticity, income elasticity, and cross-price elasticity of demand.
Unit 5: Consumer behavior: cardinal utility theory vs ordinal indifference curve approaches.

Course Code: BUA 101
Course Title: Introduction of Business
Level: 100 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Nature and scope of business enterprises, environmental factors affecting business, forms of business ownership (sole proprietorship, partnership, companies), management functions, and ethical practices in Nigeria.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Conceptual scope of business, profit motive, and social responsibilities.
Unit 2: Business environments: economic, legal, socio-cultural, and technological factors.
Unit 3: Forms of ownership: sole proprietorship, partnership, limited liability company, cooperatives.
Unit 4: Core functional areas: human resources, operations, accounting, and marketing.
Unit 5: Business planning, risk management, and government regulatory frameworks in Nigeria.

Course Code: GST 112
Course Title: Nigerian Peoples and Culture
Level: 100 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Evolution of traditional Nigerian communities, pre-colonial political systems, ethnic nationalities, inter-group interactions, colonial administrative impact, military rule, and modern socio-cultural development.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Pre-colonial political institutions in Northern, Western, and Eastern Nigeria.
Unit 2: Cultural norms, indigenous craftsmanship, religion, and social organization.
Unit 3: Colonial conquest, amalgamation of 1914, and indirect rule systems.
Unit 4: Post-independence political dynamics, nationalism, and federalism.
Unit 5: Ethnic harmony, national integration, and civic responsibility in modern Nigeria.

Course Code: NAU GST 114
Course Title: Basic Igbo Studies
Level: 100 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Study of Igbo orthography, grammar, vocabulary, proverbs, idioms, oral narratives, cultural worldview, traditional institutions, and socio-economic systems of the Igbo people.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Igbo alphabet, vowels, consonants, tone marking, and orthographic rules.
Unit 2: Parts of speech, sentence building, and translation exercises.
Unit 3: Traditional Igbo social hierarchy, title-taking (Ozo), age grades, and kingship.
Unit 4: Igbo folklore, riddles, moral values, and idiomatic expressions (Ilu).
Unit 5: Contemporary Igbo language preservation, digital literacy, and cultural heritage.

Course Code: STA 112
Course Title: Probability 1
Level: 100 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Sample spaces, events, axiomatic definition of probability, addition and multiplication rules, conditional probability, independent events, Bayes' theorem, discrete random variables, and probability mass functions.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Random experiments, elementary outcomes, events, and sample spaces.
Unit 2: Axiomatic probability foundations and basic set-theoretic theorems.
Unit 3: Conditional probability, multiplication rule, and partition of sample spaces.
Unit 4: Law of total probability and Bayes' Theorem with diagnostic applications.
Unit 5: Random variables, probability mass functions, and cumulative distribution functions.

Course Code: STA 122
Course Title: Statistical computing 1
Level: 100 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Practical statistical computing using modern tools (Excel spreadsheets, R, and SPSS). Data entry, data cleansing, tabular presentations, descriptive computations, graphical exploratory analysis, and simulation basics.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Spreadsheet fundamentals: worksheet layout, formulas, and data formatting in Excel.
Unit 2: Summary functions, pivot tables, and statistical charting.
Unit 3: Introduction to R environment: data structures (vectors, data frames, factors).
Unit 4: Descriptive metrics calculation, frequency generation, and boxplots in R & SPSS.
Unit 5: Introduction to reproducible reporting and pseudo-random number generation.

Course Code: MTH 102
Course Title: Elementary Mathematics II
Level: 100 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Trigonometric functions, radian measures, addition and factor formulas, limit of a function, differentiation from first principles, product/quotient/chain rules, integration techniques, and area under curves.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Circular trigonometric functions, trigonometric identities, and compound angles.
Unit 2: Function limits, continuity, and concept of derivative from first principles.
Unit 3: Differentiation techniques: product rule, quotient rule, and function of a function.
Unit 4: Applications of derivatives: tangents, normals, rates of change, maxima and minima.
Unit 5: Indefinite and definite integrals, integration by substitution, and basic areas.

Course Code: NAU-PHY 102
Course Title: Physics II
Level: 100 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Electrostatics, Coulomb's law, electric field and potential, capacitors and dielectrics, electric currents, Ohm's law, DC circuits, magnetic fields, electromagnetic induction, geometrical optics, and wave motion.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Electric charge, Coulomb's law, electric flux, Gauss's law, and potential.
Unit 2: Capacitance, combination of capacitors, and dielectric properties.
Unit 3: Electric current, resistance, electromotive force, and Kirchhoff's circuit rules.
Unit 4: Magnetic force on moving charges, Biot-Savart law, and Faraday's induction.
Unit 5: Reflection, refraction, lenses, mirrors, and wave interference.

Course Code: NAU-MAT 112
Course Title: Intro to actuarial Mathematics I
Level: 100 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Fundamental concepts of financial mathematics, theory of interest, simple and compound interest rates, nominal and effective rates, discount factors, present values, annuities-certain, and amortization schedules.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Time value of money, accumulation functions, and interest rate definitions.
Unit 2: Simple vs compound interest, effective vs nominal interest rates.
Unit 3: Discount rates, force of interest, and present value calculations.
Unit 4: Annuities-certain: immediate annuities, annuities-due, and perpetuities.
Unit 5: Loan amortization schedules, sinking funds, and capital redemption.

Course Code: COS 102
Course Title: Computer Programming II
Level: 100 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Principles of structured and procedural computer programming using modern high-level languages (C / Python). Data types, expressions, control structures, functions, parameter passing, arrays, and file I/O.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Language syntax, basic data types, variables, and operator precedence.
Unit 2: Selection structures: if-else branches, switch-case statements.
Unit 3: Repetition structures: while, do-while, and for loops.
Unit 4: Functions, variable scope, recursion, and parameter passing mechanisms.
Unit 5: One-dimensional and multi-dimensional arrays, string processing, and file input/output.

Course Code: NAU-BIO 102
Course Title: General Biology II
Level: 100 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Comparative study of plant and animal physiology, nutrition, gas exchange, circulatory systems, excretion, nervous coordination, hormones, reproduction, development, and environmental adaptation.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Plant nutrition: photosynthesis, mineral absorption, and transport systems.
Unit 2: Animal nutrition: digestive mechanisms and mammalian enzyme actions.
Unit 3: Respiration, gaseous exchange mechanisms, and mammalian blood circulation.
Unit 4: Osmoregulation, excretory systems, and homeostasis.
Unit 5: Nervous and endocrine coordination, sensory organs, and environmental response.

Course Code: ECO 112
Course Title: Principles of Economics II
Level: 100 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Fundamental macroeconomic theory, national income accounting (GDP, GNP, NNP), circular flow of income, aggregate demand and supply, inflation, unemployment, fiscal policy, monetary policy, and external trade.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Scope of macroeconomics and the circular flow of economic activity.
Unit 2: National income accounting: output, income, and expenditure measurement.
Unit 3: Aggregate consumption, savings function, investment multiplier, and equilibrium.
Unit 4: Money, banking institutions, and the role of the Central Bank of Nigeria.
Unit 5: Inflation types, unemployment causes, fiscal policy, and international balance of payments.

Course Code: BUA 102
Course Title: Introduction To Business II
Level: 100 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Organizational structures, operational management, production planning, total quality management, human resource management, labor unions, marketing strategies, and international business perspectives.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Organizational theory: classical, bureaucratic, and human relations models.
Unit 2: Production management: plant location, layout, inventory, and supply chain control.
Unit 3: Marketing mix: product design, pricing strategies, distribution, and promotional channels.
Unit 4: Personnel administration: recruitment, selection, training, and performance evaluation.
Unit 5: Labor relations, collective bargaining, and corporate social responsibility in Nigeria.

Course Code: ENT 211
Course Title: Entrepreneurship and Innovation 2
Level: 200 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Developing innovative entrepreneurial ventures, opportunity identification, feasibility analysis, business model canvas, financing startups, patenting, intellectual property, and venture lifecycle.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Entrepreneurial mindsets and innovation-driven opportunity evaluation.
Unit 2: Feasibility studies and the Business Model Canvas (BMC) framework.
Unit 3: Startup capitalization: angel investors, venture capital, and commercial bank loans.
Unit 4: Legal registrations, CAC processes, trademarks, and intellectual property protection.
Unit 5: Enterprise scaling, digital transformation, and risk management strategies.

Course Code: STA 211
Course Title: Probability II
Level: 200 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Discrete and continuous random variables, probability mass and density functions, cumulative distribution functions, mathematical expectation, variance, moments, moment generating functions, and standard probability models.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Univariate discrete distributions: Bernoulli, Binomial, Poisson, Geometric, Negative Binomial, Hypergeometric.
Unit 2: Univariate continuous distributions: Uniform, Normal, Exponential, Gamma, Beta, and Weibull.
Unit 3: Mathematical expectations, higher-order moments, and skewness/kurtosis measures.
Unit 4: Moment Generating Functions (MGF) and characteristic functions properties.
Unit 5: Chebyshev's Inequality, Markov's Inequality, and Law of Large Numbers intro.

Course Code: STA 221
Course Title: Statistical Inference II
Level: 200 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Sampling distributions (Student's t, Chi-Square, Snedecor's F), point estimation principles, properties of estimators (unbiasedness, consistency, efficiency, sufficiency), Method of Moments, Maximum Likelihood Estimation, and interval estimation.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Derivations and properties of Chi-Square, t, and F sampling distributions.
Unit 2: Point estimation: concept of estimator properties (unbiasedness, minimum variance, consistency).
Unit 3: Sufficiency and the Fisher-Neyman Factorization Theorem.
Unit 4: Estimation methods: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE).
Unit 5: Exact confidence intervals for one and two population means, variances, and proportions.

Course Code: STA 231
Course Title: Statistical Computing II
Level: 200 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Computational statistical algorithms using R and Python. Implementation of probability distribution calculations, pseudo-random variate generation, Monte Carlo simulations, numerical matrix operations, and regression computation.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Intermediate programming in R: control structures, loops, vectorization, and apply family.
Unit 2: Random variate generation methods: inverse transform, acceptance-rejection, Box-Muller.
Unit 3: Monte Carlo simulation of probabilistic processes and approximation of integrals.
Unit 4: Matrix algebra computations: inversion, decomposition (LU, Cholesky), and eigensystems in R.
Unit 5: Implementing custom estimation algorithms (e.g. Newton-Raphson MLE) programmatically.

Course Code: COS 201
Course Title: Computer Programming I
Level: 200 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Object-oriented programming (OOP) paradigms using modern programming languages. Classes, objects, encapsulation, data abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism, abstract classes, interfaces, and exception handling.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: OOP concepts: comparison between procedural and object-oriented paradigms.
Unit 2: Classes, object instantiation, constructors, destructors, and member access specifiers.
Unit 3: Encapsulation, information hiding, getters, and setters.
Unit 4: Single and multiple inheritance, method overriding, and polymorphism.
Unit 5: Abstract base classes, interfaces, and structured exception handling mechanisms.

Course Code: MTH 231
Course Title: Introduction to Mathematical Methods
Level: 200 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Real-valued functions of several variables, partial derivatives, directional derivatives, gradient vectors, total differentials, Taylor's series for multiple variables, extreme values, Lagrange multipliers, and multiple integrals.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Functions of two or more variables: domains, level curves, and surfaces.
Unit 2: Partial differentiation, higher order partials, and Clairaut's theorem on mixed partials.
Unit 3: Directional derivatives, gradient vector, tangent planes, and total differentials.
Unit 4: Extrema of multi-variable functions, Hessian matrix, and constrained optimization via Lagrange multipliers.
Unit 5: Double and triple integrals, Fubini's theorem, change of variables, and Jacobians.

Course Code: MTH 201
Course Title: Linear Algebra I
Level: 200 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Vector spaces over fields, subspaces, linear span, linear independence, basis, dimension, linear mappings, matrix representations of linear mappings, rank-nullity theorem, systems of linear equations, and determinants.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Vector space axioms over fields, linear combinations, and subspaces.
Unit 2: Linear dependence, linear independence, spanning sets, bases, and finite dimensionality.
Unit 3: Linear transformations: kernel, image, Rank-Nullity Theorem, and isomorphisms.
Unit 4: Matrix representation of linear transformations and change of basis matrices.
Unit 5: Systems of linear equations: Gaussian elimination, echelon forms, rank, and determinants.

Course Code: ECO 211
Course Title: Micro Economics I
Level: 200 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Intermediate microeconomic analysis: axiomatic consumer theory, utility maximization, Marshallian and Hicksian demand functions, Slutsky equation, production functions, cost minimization, and perfect competition.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Axioms of consumer preference, budget constraints, and utility functions.
Unit 2: Constrained utility maximization, Marshallian vs Compensated (Hicksian) demand.
Unit 3: Slutsky decomposition into income and substitution effects.
Unit 4: Production functions: Isoquants, Marginal Rate of Technical Substitution (MRTS), and Returns to Scale.
Unit 5: Cost function derivations (short-run vs long-run) and profit maximization in competitive markets.

Course Code: IFT 211
Course Title: Digital Logic Design
Level: 200 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Boolean algebra, truth tables, logic gates, minimization of Boolean expressions using Karnaugh maps and Quine-McCluskey, combinational logic circuits (adders, multiplexers, decoders), and sequential circuits.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Binary logic, Boolean postulates, De Morgan's laws, and standard forms (SOP, POS).
Unit 2: Logic gate implementations: AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR, XNOR.
Unit 3: Simplification techniques: Karnaugh maps up to 5 variables and prime implicants.
Unit 4: Combinational circuits: half/full adders, subtractors, magnitude comparators, multiplexers, decoders.
Unit 5: Latches, flip-flops (SR, JK, D, T), clocking, counters, and basic register design.

Course Code: AMS 101
Course Title: Principles of Management
Level: 200 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Theoretical evolution of administrative thought, classical management, behavioral human relations, systems theory, contingency approach, and managerial functions: planning, organizing, staffing, leading, and controlling.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Nature, purpose, and universal principles of administrative management.
Unit 2: Historical schools: Scientific Management (Taylor), Administrative (Fayol), and Bureaucratic (Weber).
Unit 3: Strategic and operational planning: MBO, SWOT analysis, and decision-making techniques.
Unit 4: Organizational structure: centralization vs decentralization, span of control, and departmentalization.
Unit 5: Leadership styles, motivational frameworks (Maslow, Herzberg), and controlling systems.

Course Code: GST 212
Course Title: Philosophy, Logic, and Human Existence
Level: 200 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Scope and major branches of philosophy (epistemology, metaphysics, ethics, aesthetics), logical reasoning, valid argument deduction, propositional logic, categorical syllogisms, informal fallacies, and existential questions.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: The nature, method, and branches of philosophical inquiry.
Unit 2: Epistemology: sources and justification of human knowledge (empiricism vs rationalism).
Unit 3: Propositional logic, connectives, truth tables, and validity testing.
Unit 4: Categorical syllogisms, Euler diagrams, and formal/informal logical fallacies.
Unit 5: Philosophical foundations of science, human rights, justice, and existential meaning.

Course Code: STA 202
Course Title: Statistics for Physical Sciences & Engineering
Level: 200 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Application of statistical methods to engineering and physical science domains: experimental measurement errors, propagation of errors, curve fitting, regression, hypothesis testing, reliability, and quality control.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Physical measurements, random and systematic errors, and error propagation formulas.
Unit 2: Probability models for engineering phenomena (Weibull, Lognormal, Extreme Value distributions).
Unit 3: Method of least squares, linear and polynomial curve fitting for calibration.
Unit 4: Hypothesis tests for material strength, variance comparisons, and ANOVA in lab trials.
Unit 5: Statistical process control, Shewhart charts, and system reliability analysis.

Course Code: STA 212
Course Title: Introduction to Social & Economic Statistics
Level: 200 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Official statistical systems, National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) structure, national accounts, index numbers (Laspeyres, Paasche, Fisher), Consumer Price Index (CPI), inflation metrics, vital statistics, and demographic indicators.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: National official statistical architecture: NBS, statistical coordination, and data governance.
Unit 2: Index numbers: simple, weighted aggregate, price and quantity relatives, tests of consistency.
Unit 3: Consumer Price Index (CPI) methodology, inflation computation, and purchasing power parity.
Unit 4: Vital statistics: crude and age-specific birth/death rates, infant mortality, and fertility indices.
Unit 5: Population census procedures, socio-economic surveys, and poverty headcount metrics.

Course Code: NAU-STA 214
Course Title: Probability and Probability Distribution
Level: 200 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Bivariate probability distributions, joint probability mass and density functions, marginal and conditional distributions, stochastic independence, covariance, correlation coefficient, conditional expectation, and bivariate normal distribution.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Joint probability distributions of discrete and continuous random variables.
Unit 2: Marginal distributions and conditional probability distributions.
Unit 3: Stochastic independence of random variables and conditional expectation.
Unit 4: Covariance, Pearson correlation coefficient, and properties of variance of sums.
Unit 5: Bivariate transformation techniques and the Bivariate Normal Distribution derivation.

Course Code: COS 202
Course Title: Computer Programming II
Level: 200 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Fundamental data structures and algorithmic complexity. Memory representation, linked lists (singly, doubly), stacks, queues, binary search trees, sorting algorithms (quicksort, mergesort), and graph traversal.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Abstract Data Types (ADT) and algorithmic Big-O asymptotic notation.
Unit 2: Dynamic memory allocation, pointer manipulation, and singly/doubly linked lists.
Unit 3: Stacks and queues: array/pointer implementations, postfix evaluations, and recursion.
Unit 4: Non-linear structures: binary trees, binary search trees, and tree traversals (in/pre/post).
Unit 5: Searching and sorting algorithms: insertion, selection, quicksort, mergesort, and hash tables.

Course Code: NAU-MTH 202
Course Title: Elementary Differential Equation II
Level: 200 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Second-order linear ordinary differential equations with constant coefficients, undetermined coefficients, variation of parameters, Cauchy-Euler equations, series solutions, Frobenius method, and Laplace transforms.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Second order homogeneous linear ODEs: auxiliary equation and complementary functions.
Unit 2: Non-homogeneous linear ODEs: Method of Undetermined Coefficients and Variation of Parameters.
Unit 3: Cauchy-Euler differential equations and systems of first-order linear ODEs.
Unit 4: Power series solutions around ordinary and regular singular points (Frobenius method).
Unit 5: Laplace transformation, inverse transforms, convolution theorem, and initial value problems.

Course Code: STA 299
Course Title: Industrial Training
Level: 200 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Supervised vacation practical industrial attachment. Exposure to industrial work settings, practical data entry, database logging, statistical summary reporting, and documentation in government, corporate, or research institutions.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Industrial placement orientation, workplace ethics, and safety protocols.
Unit 2: Practical data acquisition, logging, and database auditing workflows.
Unit 3: Applied spreadsheet analysis and weekly statistical logbook maintenance.
Unit 4: Collaborative departmental data presentation and preliminary statistical reporting.
Unit 5: Comprehensive industrial training logbook review and oral departmental evaluation.

Course Code: MTH 204
Course Title: Linear Algebra II
Level: 200 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors, characteristic polynomials, minimal polynomials, Cayley-Hamilton theorem, matrix diagonalization, inner product spaces, Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization process, and quadratic forms.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Characteristic values and characteristic vectors of linear operators.
Unit 2: Characteristic polynomial, algebraic/geometric multiplicity, and Cayley-Hamilton theorem.
Unit 3: Diagonalizability criteria and Jordan Canonical Forms introduction.
Unit 4: Real and complex inner product spaces, Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, and orthogonality.
Unit 5: Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization procedure, orthogonal projections, and symmetric matrices.

Course Code: MTH 212
Course Title: Introduction to Actuarial Mathematics
Level: 200 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Survival models, force of mortality, life tables, life assurance contracts (whole life, term, endowment), life annuities, net premium determination, and introduction to policy benefit reserves.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Survival distributions, future lifetime random variables, and force of mortality.
Unit 2: Life table construction: lx, dx, qx, px, and fractional age assumptions.
Unit 3: Life assurances: whole life, term assurance, endowment, and pure endowment present values.
Unit 4: Life annuities: continuous, immediate, and due annuity expectations.
Unit 5: Equivalence principle, net single and level annual premium calculations, and reserves.

Course Code: ECO 212
Course Title: Micro Economics II
Level: 200 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Market structures: monopoly pricing, price discrimination, monopolistic competition, oligopoly models (Cournot, Bertrand, Stackelberg), game theory introduction, general equilibrium, and welfare economics.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Pure monopoly equilibrium, deadweight loss, and first/second/third degree price discrimination.
Unit 2: Monopolistic competition: short-run and long-run Chamberlinian equilibrium.
Unit 3: Oligopoly theories: Cournot, Bertrand, and Stackelberg leader-follower duopoly models.
Unit 4: Strategic game theory: normal form games, dominant strategies, and Nash Equilibrium.
Unit 5: General equilibrium: Edgeworth box, Pareto optimality, market failures, and externalities.

Course Code: STA 311
Course Title: Probability III
Level: 300 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Advanced probability spaces, distributions of functions of random variables, Jacobian transformation techniques, order statistics and their distributions, multivariate distributions, characteristic functions, and probability inequalities.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Probability spaces, sigma-algebras, Borel sets, and probability measures.
Unit 2: Jacobians of single and multi-variable transformations of random variables.
Unit 3: Order statistics: joint and marginal distributions of smallest, largest, and median values.
Unit 4: Characteristic functions, inversion formula, and uniqueness theorems.
Unit 5: Modes of convergence (in probability, almost surely, in distribution) and Central Limit Theorem.

Course Code: STA 321
Course Title: Statistical Inference III
Level: 300 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Point estimation theory: Fisher information, Cramer-Rao Lower Bound (CRLB), efficiency, complete and sufficient statistics, Rao-Blackwell Theorem, Lehmann-Scheffe Theorem, UMVUE, and asymptotic properties.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Likelihood function, score function, and Fisher Information matrix.
Unit 2: Cramer-Rao Lower Bound regularity conditions and proof for unbiased estimators.
Unit 3: Exponential family of probability distributions and complete sufficient statistics.
Unit 4: Rao-Blackwellization and Lehmann-Scheffe theorem for finding UMVUE estimators.
Unit 5: Asymptotic efficiency and normality of Maximum Likelihood Estimators.

Course Code: STA 331
Course Title: Statistical Computing III
Level: 300 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Advanced statistical computing and modeling in R and Python. Resampling methods (bootstrap, jackknife), EM algorithm, numerical optimization (Nelder-Mead, BFGS), Bayesian MCMC basics, and interactive markdown reporting.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Numerical optimization: Newton-Raphson, Fisher scoring, and gradient descent.
Unit 2: Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm for missing data and mixture models.
Unit 3: Non-parametric bootstrap: standard error, bias estimation, and BCa confidence intervals.
Unit 4: Jackknife resampling and cross-validation techniques for model selection.
Unit 5: Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) intro: Metropolis-Hastings and Gibbs sampling.

Course Code: NAU-STA 341
Course Title: Regression Analysis I
Level: 300 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Simple and multiple linear regression, Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) estimation in matrix notation, Gauss-Markov theorem, coefficient of determination, hypothesis testing on regression coefficients, and ANOVA in regression.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Simple linear regression: assumptions, derivation of OLS estimators, and properties.
Unit 2: Multiple linear regression in matrix notation: Y = Xb + e, normal equations, and (X'X)^-1.
Unit 3: Gauss-Markov theorem and proof that OLS is BLUE (Best Linear Unbiased Estimator).
Unit 4: Tests of significance: t-tests for coefficients, overall F-test, and R-squared/adjusted R-squared.
Unit 5: Confidence intervals and prediction intervals for mean responses and individual forecasts.

Course Code: NAU-STA 351
Course Title: Analysis of Variance I
Level: 300 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Linear statistical models, fixed and random effects, one-way classification, Completely Randomized Design (CRD), two-way classification with and without interaction, Randomized Complete Block Design (RCBD), and Latin Square Design (LSD).
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Linear models: fixed, random, and mixed effects model definitions.
Unit 2: One-way ANOVA and Completely Randomized Design (CRD) partition of sums of squares.
Unit 3: Post-hoc multiple comparison tests: Fisher's LSD, Tukey's HSD, Duncan's Multiple Range, Scheffe's.
Unit 4: Two-way ANOVA without interaction: RCBD model, relative efficiency, and missing plots.
Unit 5: Latin Square Design: model specification, layout, ANOVA table, and efficiency relative to CRD.

Course Code: NAU-STA 361
Course Title: Demography
Level: 300 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Demographic data collection, errors in demographic data, mortality analysis, fertility indices, reproduction rates, complete and abridged life tables, population growth models, population estimation, and demographic transition.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Nature of demography, sources of data, census procedures, and post-enumeration surveys.
Unit 2: Evaluation of age and sex data: Whipple's Index, Myers' Blended Index, and UN Age-Sex Index.
Unit 3: Measures of mortality: crude death rate, age-specific death rates, infant mortality, and standardization.
Unit 4: Measures of fertility: CBR, GFR, ASFR, Total Fertility Rate (TFR), GRR, and NRR.
Unit 5: Life tables: construction of complete/abridged life tables, stationary populations, and projections.

Course Code: NAU-STA 371
Course Title: Operations Research I
Level: 300 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Introduction to operations research, mathematical modeling, Linear Programming (LP) formulation, graphical solution method, the Simplex algorithm, artificial variable techniques (Big M, Two-Phase), and duality theory.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: History, methodology, and mathematical formulation of Linear Programming problems.
Unit 2: Graphical solution method for two-variable linear optimization models.
Unit 3: The Simplex algorithm: tableau construction, pivot operations, and optimality criteria.
Unit 4: Artificial variable methods: Big-M method and Two-Phase Simplex technique.
Unit 5: Duality in linear programming: primal-dual relationships, economic interpretation, and dual simplex.

Course Code: NAU-STA 381
Course Title: Biometry
Level: 300 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Statistical methods in biological, agricultural, and medical research: bioassays, direct and indirect assays, parallel-line and slope-ratio assays, quantal response assays, probit and logit analysis, LD50 estimation, and clinical trials.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Scope of biometry and characteristics of biological variation.
Unit 2: Principles of biological assay: direct assays and precision estimation.
Unit 3: Quantitative indirect assays: parallel-line assays and slope-ratio assays.
Unit 4: Quantal response assays: dose-response curves, Probit transformation, Logit model, and LD50/ED50.
Unit 5: Clinical trial design: randomization, blinding, ethical considerations, and cross-over designs.

Course Code: GST 312
Course Title: Peace and Conflict Resolution
Level: 300 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Conflict analysis, root causes of ethnic, religious, and political disputes in Africa, conflict mapping, crisis de-escalation, alternative dispute resolution (ADR), negotiation, mediation, arbitration, and peacebuilding.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Conceptual definitions of peace, conflict, violence, and security.
Unit 2: Theories of conflict: structural, biological, economic, and human needs theories.
Unit 3: Conflict dynamics in Nigeria: resource control, ethnicity, religious clashes, and terrorism.
Unit 4: Conflict transformation mechanisms: communication, negotiation, mediation, and arbitration.
Unit 5: Post-conflict peacebuilding, disarmament, demobilization, rehabilitation, and rule of law.

Course Code: ENT 312
Course Title: Venture Creation
Level: 300 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Practical enterprise creation, commercialization of scientific ideas, business plan preparation, financial forecasting, product prototyping, digital marketing, corporate regulatory compliance, and managing sustainable ventures.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Ideation, lean startup methodologies, and minimal viable product (MVP) design.
Unit 2: Market research, customer discovery, competitor benchmarking, and value propositions.
Unit 3: Financial planning: cash flow statements, break-even analysis, and balance sheet forecasting.
Unit 4: Operational setup: supply chains, intellectual property filing, and CAC incorporation.
Unit 5: Pitching to investors, venture governance, scaling strategies, and exit avenues.

Course Code: STA 312
Course Title: Distribution theory I
Level: 300 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Advanced distribution theory: Pearson system of distributions, compound distributions, truncated distributions, convolutions of random variables, order statistics distributions, and multivariate probability families.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: The Pearson family of frequency curves: differential equation and classification of types.
Unit 2: Compound and mixture distributions: Poisson-Gamma (Negative Binomial), Binomial-Beta.
Unit 3: Truncated distributions: left, right, and doubly truncated probability models.
Unit 4: Sums and convolutions of independent random variables using transforms.
Unit 5: Sampling distributions derived from normal populations and non-central distributions.

Course Code: STA 324
Course Title: Survey methods and sampling theory
Level: 300 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Principles and practice of sample surveys: survey planning, questionnaire design, sampling and non-sampling errors, Simple Random Sampling (SRS), Stratified Random Sampling, optimum allocation, Systematic Sampling, and Cluster Sampling.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Planning and execution of sample surveys, sampling frame, questionnaire design, and pre-testing.
Unit 2: Simple Random Sampling (SRSWOR & SRSWR): estimation of population mean, total, and variances.
Unit 3: Stratified Random Sampling: proportional allocation, Neyman allocation, and gain in precision.
Unit 4: Systematic sampling: circular and linear systematic selection, and comparison with SRS.
Unit 5: Cluster sampling with equal clusters, two-stage sampling, and non-sampling error reduction.

Course Code: NAU-STA 322
Course Title: Statistical Quality Control I
Level: 300 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Statistical quality control philosophy, control charts for variables (X-bar, R, and S charts), control charts for attributes (p, np, c, and u charts), operating characteristic curves, process capability analysis, and acceptance sampling.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Quality concepts, Deming philosophy, chance and assignable causes of process variation.
Unit 2: Shewhart control charts for variables: X-bar and R charts, trial control limits, and interpretation.
Unit 3: Control charts for attributes: fraction nonconforming (p and np charts) and defects (c and u charts).
Unit 4: Process capability indices: Cp, Cpk, and Cpm calculations and interpretations.
Unit 5: Acceptance sampling for attributes: single sampling plans, OC curves, AQL, and LTPD.

Course Code: NAU-STA 362
Course Title: Statistical Methods In Epidemiology
Level: 300 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Statistical methods in public health: epidemiological study designs (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional), measures of disease occurrence, measures of association (relative risk, odds ratio), confounding, standardization, and survival curves.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Fundamental principles of epidemiology, disease causation, and observational study designs.
Unit 2: Measures of disease frequency: incidence rate, incidence proportion (risk), and prevalence.
Unit 3: Measures of association: Risk Ratio (RR), Odds Ratio (OR), Attributable Risk, and population AR.
Unit 4: Confounding and interaction (effect modification): Mantel-Haenszel stratified methods.
Unit 5: Standardization of rates (direct and indirect) and introduction to Kaplan-Meier survival curves.

Course Code: NAU-STA 342
Course Title: Statistical Application of Matrix Algebra
Level: 300 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Matrix operations in statistical theory: partitioned matrices, determinants, trace properties, generalized inverses (Moore-Penrose), idempotent matrices, quadratic forms, eigenvalues, spectral decomposition, and distributions of quadratic forms.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Review of matrix operations: partitioned matrices, Kronecker products, trace, and rank.
Unit 2: Generalized inverses (g-inverses): definitions, Moore-Penrose inverse, and solving linear systems.
Unit 3: Idempotent matrices, projection operators, and orthogonal projections in linear models.
Unit 4: Quadratic forms: positive definiteness, spectral decomposition, and differentiation with respect to vectors.
Unit 5: Distribution of quadratic forms, Cochran's Theorem, and independence of linear and quadratic forms.

Course Code: STA 399
Course Title: Industrial Attachment
Level: 300 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Supervised Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme (SIWES). Three months of practical professional attachment undertaken twice (after 200L second semester and after 300L second semester) in industry, financial banks, research institutes, or statistical agencies applying quantitative skills to live data operations.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Industrial placement registration, employer orientation, and industrial safety compliance.
Unit 2: Active operational engagement in statistical data collection, cleaning, and database reporting.
Unit 3: Weekly logbook documentation of technical statistical tasks, programming scripts, and analyses.
Unit 4: Institutional supervisory visits and mid-attachment performance appraisals.
Unit 5: Submission of comprehensive SIWES technical report and oral defense before departmental board.

Course Code: STA 411
Course Title: Probability IV
Level: 400 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Measure-theoretic probability foundations: sigma-fields, measurable spaces, probability measures, Lebesgue-Stieltjes integrals, Radon-Nikodym theorem, conditional expectation given a sigma-field, martingales, and convergence theorems.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Measure theory foundations: algebras, sigma-algebras, Borel fields, and outer measures.
Unit 2: Measurable functions, random variables as measurable mappings, and integration theory.
Unit 3: Monotone Convergence Theorem, Fatou's Lemma, and Lebesgue Dominated Convergence Theorem.
Unit 4: Radon-Nikodym derivative and conditional expectation with respect to sub-sigma-fields.
Unit 5: Martingales: discrete-parameter sub-martingales, super-martingales, and Doob's Optional Stopping Theorem.

Course Code: STA 413
Course Title: Statistical Inference IV
Level: 400 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Advanced hypothesis testing theory: Neyman-Pearson fundamental lemma, Uniformly Most Powerful (UMP) tests, monotone likelihood ratio (MLR) property, unbiased tests (UMPU), Likelihood Ratio Tests (LRT), and sequential probability ratio tests.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: General formulation of statistical hypothesis testing and randomized test functions.
Unit 2: Neyman-Pearson Fundamental Lemma: statement, proof, and construction of Most Powerful tests.
Unit 3: Families with Monotone Likelihood Ratio (MLR) and derivation of one-sided UMP tests.
Unit 4: Two-sided hypotheses, concept of unbiasedness, and Uniformly Most Powerful Unbiased (UMPU) tests.
Unit 5: Likelihood Ratio Test (LRT) construction, asymptotic Chi-Square distribution, and Wald's SPRT.

Course Code: NAU-STA 421
Course Title: Times Analysis
Level: 400 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Time Series Analysis: stationary and non-stationary processes, autocovariance and autocorrelation functions (ACF/PACF), Box-Jenkins AR, MA, ARMA, and ARIMA models, unit root testing, spectral analysis, and forecasting.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Time series components, stationarity definitions (strict vs weak), autocovariance, and ACF.
Unit 2: Autoregressive (AR), Moving Average (MA), and mixed ARMA stochastic processes and conditions.
Unit 3: Non-stationary series: difference-stationarity, ARIMA models, and Box-Jenkins three-stage methodology.
Unit 4: Unit root tests: Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) and Phillips-Perron tests for stationarity.
Unit 5: Forecasting techniques, prediction error variance, and introduction to ARCH/GARCH volatility models.

Course Code: NAU-STA 441
Course Title: Regression Analysis II
Level: 400 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Advanced regression methodology: multicollinearity diagnostics, ridge regression, LASSO, model selection criteria (AIC, BIC, Mallows' Cp), residual diagnostics, non-linear regression, and Generalized Linear Models (GLMs).
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Multicollinearity: detection (VIF, Condition Number) and remedial ridge/lasso shrinkage methods.
Unit 2: Regression model diagnostics: studentized residuals, leverage values, Cook's distance, and outliers.
Unit 3: Model selection strategies: stepwise regression, best subsets, AIC, BIC, and cross-validation.
Unit 4: Polynomial and non-linear regression estimation via Gauss-Newton iterative algorithms.
Unit 5: Generalized Linear Models (GLMs): link functions, logistic regression, and Poisson regression.

Course Code: NAU-STA 451
Course Title: Design And Analysis of Experiment
Level: 400 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Advanced experimental design: factorial experiment structures (2^k and 3^k series), complete and partial confounding, fractional factorial replication, split-plot designs, nested designs, and Response Surface Methodology (RSM).
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Factorial designs: main effects, two-factor and three-factor interactions in 2^k factorials.
Unit 2: Confounding in 2^k factorials: complete confounding, partial confounding, and defining contrasts.
Unit 3: Fractional factorial designs: 2^(k-p) designs, resolution III, IV, and V, and alias structures.
Unit 4: Split-plot and split-block experimental layouts, models, and ANOVA partitioning.
Unit 5: Response Surface Methodology: central composite designs, steepest ascent, and stationary points.

Course Code: NAU-STA 461
Course Title: Multivariate Analysis I
Level: 400 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Multivariate normal distributions, properties of random vectors and covariance matrices, Hotelling's T-squared distribution, testing multivariate hypotheses on mean vectors, Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA), and Principal Component Analysis.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Multivariate random vectors: mean vector, dispersion matrix, and multivariate normal density.
Unit 2: Sampling distributions of sample mean vector and Wishart distribution of sample covariance matrix.
Unit 3: Hotelling's T-squared statistic: one-sample and two-sample tests for mean vectors.
Unit 4: One-way and two-way MANOVA: Wilks' Lambda, Pillai's trace, Hotelling-Lawley trace, and Roy's root.
Unit 5: Principal Component Analysis (PCA): algebraic derivation, eigenvalue scree plots, and data reduction.

Course Code: NAU-STA 491
Course Title: Seminar
Level: 400 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 1
Description: Individual undergraduate academic research seminar. Literature synthesis on a cutting-edge statistical theory or application, written seminar report compilation, and oral presentation before the departmental seminar panel.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Scientific research methodology, topic formulation, and scholarly literature search.
Unit 2: Critical appraisal of published peer-reviewed statistical literature.
Unit 3: Scientific paper structuring, LaTeX / Markdown typesetting, and academic citation standards.
Unit 4: Slide design, scientific storytelling, and visual data representation.
Unit 5: Oral seminar delivery, defense of methodology, and question-and-answer engagement.

Course Code: NAU-STA 471
Course Title: Operations Research II
Level: 400 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Advanced operations research techniques: Integer Programming (Branch and Bound, Cutting Plane), Dynamic Programming, Game Theory (two-person zero-sum, saddle points), Queuing Theory (M/M/1, M/M/c), and Project Network Scheduling (CPM/PERT).
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Integer Linear Programming: Gomory's cutting plane algorithm and Branch-and-Bound methods.
Unit 2: Dynamic programming: Bellman's principle of optimality, recursive equations, and stage decisions.
Unit 3: Theory of games: minimax theorem, mixed strategies, linear programming formulation of games.
Unit 4: Queuing models: Poisson arrivals, exponential service times, M/M/1 and M/M/k queuing equations.
Unit 5: Project scheduling: network diagrams, critical path method (CPM), and PERT probabilistic analysis.

Course Code: NAU-STA 481
Course Title: Statistical Quality Control I
Level: 400 Level (Semester 1)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Advanced quality engineering: Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) control charts, Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (EWMA) charts, multivariate quality control charts (Hotelling's T^2 charts), continuous sampling plans, and Six Sigma DMAIC methodologies.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Advanced memory-type control charts: tabular and V-mask Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) charts.
Unit 2: Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (EWMA) control charts for detecting small process shifts.
Unit 3: Multivariate quality control: Hotelling's T-squared control chart for correlated quality characteristics.
Unit 4: Continuous sampling inspection plans (CSP-1, CSP-2) and sequential sampling plans.
Unit 5: Six Sigma quality framework: DMAIC cycle, gauge repeatability & reproducibility (R&R) studies.

Course Code: STA 412
Course Title: Distribution Theory II
Level: 400 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Multivariate continuous distributions: Multivariate Normal, Wishart distribution, Hotelling's T^2 distribution, distribution of quadratic forms, non-central Chi-square, non-central t and F, and asymptotic distribution theorems.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Matrix-variate distributions and properties of the Wishart distribution.
Unit 2: Derivation and properties of Hotelling's T-squared distribution.
Unit 3: Non-central probability distributions: non-central Chi-Square, non-central t, and non-central F.
Unit 4: Distributions of linear and quadratic forms under multivariate normality.
Unit 5: Asymptotic expansion of distributions, delta method, and saddle-point approximations.

Course Code: STA 422
Course Title: Logical Background of Statistics and Decision Theory
Level: 400 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 3
Description: Philosophical and logical foundations of statistical inference, inductive logic, subjective vs objective probability, Bayesian decision theory, prior and posterior distributions, loss functions, risk functions, minimax and Bayes rules.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Inductive logic, philosophical debates on probability (classical, frequentist, subjective/Bayesian).
Unit 2: Statistical decision problem components: states of nature, actions, loss functions, and risk.
Unit 3: Utility theory axioms, von Neumann-Morgenstern utility, and decision criteria under uncertainty.
Unit 4: Bayesian decision principles: conjugate priors, posterior risk, and optimal Bayes decision rules.
Unit 5: Minimax decision criterion, admissible decision rules, and randomized decision procedures.

Course Code: NAU-STA 424
Course Title: Stochastic Processes
Level: 400 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Markov chains in discrete and continuous time, transition probability matrices, Chapman-Kolmogorov equations, classification of states, stationary distributions, Poisson processes, birth-and-death processes, and queuing applications.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Definition of stochastic processes, index sets, state spaces, and Markov property.
Unit 2: Discrete-time Markov Chains: transition probability matrix and Chapman-Kolmogorov equations.
Unit 3: Classification of states: periodicity, recurrence, transience, absorbing states, and ergodicity.
Unit 4: Stationary distributions and long-run limiting behavior of irreducible recurrent chains.
Unit 5: Continuous-time Markov processes: Poisson process, pure birth, and birth-and-death processes.

Course Code: NAU-STA 432
Course Title: Non–parametric Methods
Level: 400 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Distribution-free statistical methods: order statistics, Sign test, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test, Mann-Whitney U test, Kruskal-Wallis one-way ANOVA by ranks, Friedman two-way ANOVA, Kendall's tau, Spearman's rank correlation, and Kolmogorov-Smirnov goodness-of-fit.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Concepts of non-parametric vs parametric inference, empirical distribution function.
Unit 2: One-sample tests: Sign test, Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test, and Kolmogorov-Smirnov one-sample test.
Unit 3: Two independent sample tests: Mann-Whitney U test and Kolmogorov-Smirnov two-sample test.
Unit 4: K-sample tests: Kruskal-Wallis test for independent samples and Friedman test for paired data.
Unit 5: Measures of association: Spearman's rank correlation (rho) and Kendall's rank correlation (tau).

Course Code: NAU-STA 442
Course Title: Multivariate Analysis II
Level: 400 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Advanced multivariate data analysis: Factor Analysis (orthogonal and oblique rotations), Canonical Correlation Analysis, Linear and Quadratic Discriminant Analysis, Cluster Analysis (hierarchical and k-means), and Multidimensional Scaling.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Exploratory and confirmatory Factor Analysis: principal factor method, varimax rotation, factor scores.
Unit 2: Canonical Correlation Analysis: canonical variates, canonical correlations, and significance tests.
Unit 3: Discriminant Analysis: Fisher's linear discriminant function, classification rules, and error rates.
Unit 4: Cluster Analysis: distance metrics, hierarchical clustering (Ward, complete, average), and K-means.
Unit 5: Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) and Correspondence Analysis for categorical dimensionality reduction.

Course Code: NAU-STA 452
Course Title: Analysis of Variance II
Level: 400 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 2
Description: Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA), nested and hierarchical designs, unbalanced ANOVA, mixed and random effects linear models, variance components estimation (ANOVA method, REML), and repeated measures ANOVA.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA): single covariate linear model, test of parallel slopes, adjusted means.
Unit 2: Nested (hierarchical) classification designs: two-stage nested model and ANOVA table.
Unit 3: Unbalanced two-way ANOVA: exact method of fitting constants and weighted squares of means.
Unit 4: Random effects and mixed models: expected mean squares (EMS) and variance components estimation via REML.
Unit 5: Repeated measures ANOVA: sphericity assumption, Mauchly's test, and Greenhouse-Geisser correction.

Course Code: STA 499
Course Title: Project
Level: 400 Level (Semester 2)
Credit Units: 6
Description: Supervised individual final year research project. Independent empirical data collection, statistical modeling, simulation or theoretical contribution, written dissertation submission, and oral defense before external and internal boards.
Syllabus Outline: Unit 1: Topic selection, hypothesis formulation, research proposal, and supervisor assignment.
Unit 2: Comprehensive literature review and conceptual statistical framework definition.
Unit 3: Methodology formulation, sampling design, data acquisition, and quality validation.
Unit 4: Advanced statistical computation, modeling, hypothesis testing, and empirical interpretations.
Unit 5: Final bound dissertation submission and oral viva voce defense before the examination panel.

Biography & Background: Dr. Samuel Ugochukwu Enogwe is a distinguished academic and researcher with extensive expertise in Statistics, Operations Research, and Economics. He began his academic journey at the Federal Polytechnic Nekede, Owerri, Nigeria, earning a Higher National Diploma (HND) in Statistics with Distinction in November 2011. He proceeded to Michael Okpara University of Agriculture, Umudike, where he obtained a B.Sc. in Statistics with First Class Honours in November 2015, followed by an M.Sc. in Operations Research in August 2018, graduating as the Overall Best M.Sc. student with a perfect C.G.P.A. of 5.00/5.00. He subsequently earned a Ph.D. in Statistics (Operations Research) from Nnamdi Azikiwe University, Awka, in January 2023, receiving recognition as the Best Graduating Ph.D. student of the Department of Statistics for the 2022/2023 session. Complementing his postgraduate studies, he obtained a Postgraduate Diploma (PGD) in Economics with Distinction from Michael Okpara University of Agriculture, Umudike, in January 2026 and is currently pursuing a Master’s degree in Development Economics at the same institution. Dr. Enogwe’s research interests span Statistics, Operations Research, and Economics. His work focuses on developing Batch Arrival Non-Markovian queueing models, designing new statistical distributions for real-world applications, and exploring econometric modeling in development economics. He is highly proficient in statistical and computational tools, including R, Python, and other software packages essential for data-driven research. He has deployed innovative teaching and learning methods to make Statistics accessible and engaging for students and has served as an internal examiner for both Masters’ degree and Ph.D. students. He began his lecturing career at the Department of Mathematics/Statistics, Federal Polytechnic Nekede, Owerri, where he contributed significantly to teaching, research, and community development. He joined Michael Okpara University of Agriculture, Umudike, in 2019 and has been instrumental in the growth and development of the Department of Statistics and the University at large. He has been teaching statistical computing courses in the Department, helping students to utilize various statistical software for data analysis. He has also served as a resource person for MOUAU-LISA, IMSU-LISA, NAU-LISA, and Federal Polytechnic Oko, providing training on R and Python for Data Science. Dr. Enogwe has made significant contributions to university governance and academic service. He serves as the Secretary of the Departmental Academic Quality Assurance Committee (2024–present), member of the Departmental Postgraduate Board (2023–present), and Level Adviser (2021–present). Additionally, he is a member of Examination Moderation Committee (2021-present), Curriculum Review and Development Committee (2021-present), and Documentation & Library Committee for Accreditation (2021-present), Statistics Course Recovery & Harmonization Committee (2025–present), Chairman of the Secretarial sub-committee for the COLPAS Maiden Conference (2025–present), and College Representative to the School of General Studies (2025–present), MOUAU. He currently serves as Publicity Secretary of the Institute of Operational Research and Management Science of Nigeria (IORMS) and previously held the position of Assistant General Secretary (2023–2025). He has served as member Local Organizing Committee (LOC) of Several Conferences. Dr. Enogwe is an active researcher with over 31 peer-reviewed journal publications and 33 conference papers. He is a member of several professional organizations, including the Chartered Institute of Statisticians of Nigeria (CISON), the Professional Statisticians of Nigeria (PSSN), and the International Biometric Society (IBS). He is happily married to Mrs. Chinenye Eucharia Samuel-Enogwe, an English Language expert, and they enjoy a strong and flourishing family life grounded in faith and mutual support.

Category: SIWES

1. Prokaryotic Cellular Organization
The most fundamental characteristic of bacteria is their prokaryotic cellular organization. Unlike
eukaryotic organisms, bacteria lack a true nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles such as

The absence of membrane-bound organelles does not imply structural simplicity in function. Rather,
bacteria possess highly efficient cellular systems that enable them to perform all essential life processes,
including metabolism, growth, reproduction, and adaptation to environmental changes. Cellular
respiration, for example, occurs on the plasma membrane rather than within mitochondria.

Bacteria are generally microscopic organisms, with most species measuring between 0.5 and 5.0

Although bacterial cells are structurally less complex than eukaryotic cells, they possess all the essential

3. Unicellular Nature
Bacteria are unicellular organisms, meaning that each cell functions as a complete and independent living
unit capable of carrying out all vital physiological processes. Unlike multicellular organisms that possess

arrangements often serve as important diagnostic features during microscopic examination and
contribute significantly to bacterial identification.
The unicellular organization of bacteria allows rapid adaptation to environmental changes because each

4. Peptidoglycan Cell Wall Structure
Most bacteria possess a rigid cell wall that surrounds the plasma membrane and provides structural
integrity to the cell. The principal component of the bacterial cell wall is peptidoglycan, a complex
macromolecule composed of alternating sugar residues cross-linked by short peptide chains.
The cell wall performs several essential functions. It maintains cellular shape, protects against mechanical
damage, prevents osmotic lysis, and contributes to bacterial survival in diverse environments. Because
bacterial cytoplasm typically contains a higher concentration of dissolved substances than the
surrounding environment, water tends to enter the cell by osmosis.

ecological and physiological requirements. Cell morphology is often genetically determined and

6. Motility and Movement
Many bacterial species possess the ability to move actively through their environment. Motility is primarily
mediated by flagella, which are long, filamentous appendages extending from the cell surface. The
bacterial flagellum functions as a rotary motor capable of propelling the cell through liquid environments.
Motility provides significant ecological advantages. It enables bacteria to move toward favorable
conditions and away from harmful substances, a phenomenon known as taxis. Chemotaxis, for example,
refers to movement in response to chemical gradients, allowing bacteria to locate nutrients and avoid
toxic compounds.

Some bacteria possess a single flagellum, whereas others have multiple flagella distributed in various
arrangements. Certain bacterial groups, particularly spirochetes, utilize specialized internal flagella known
as axial filaments that facilitate movement through viscous environments such as mucus and connective
tissues. The presence or absence of motility is frequently used as a distinguishing characteristic in
bacterial identification and classification.

Bacteria reproduce primarily through binary fission, an asexual process involving DNA replication followed
by division of a parent cell into two genetically identical daughter cells. Under optimal environmental
conditions, some bacterial species can divide every twenty minutes, resulting in exponential population
growth.
The process begins with replication of the bacterial chromosome. As the cell elongates, the replicated
chromosomes move apart, and a septum forms across the center of the cell. The septum eventually
develops into a new cell wall, separating the daughter cells.
Although binary fission produces genetically identical offspring, bacteria possess several mechanisms for
genetic exchange that contribute to variation and evolution.

IDENTIFICATION OF BACTERIA
Bacterial identification is the process of determining the identity of an unknown bacterial isolate through
the examination of its structural, physiological, biochemical, immunological, and genetic characteristics.
Accurate identification is essential in clinical diagnosis, epidemiological investigations, environmental
monitoring, food safety, and industrial microbiology. Because no single characteristic is sufficient for
definitive identification, microbiologists typically employ a combination of methods that collectively
provide a comprehensive understanding of bacterial identity.

6. Molecular Identification
Advances in molecular biology have revolutionized bacterial identification by allowing direct examination
of genetic material. Molecular methods provide exceptional sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy and have
become indispensable in modern microbiology. Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) enables the
amplification and detection of specific DNA sequences unique to particular bacterial species. DNA
sequencing techniques allow direct comparison of genetic information among organisms, providing
insights into evolutionary relationships and taxonomic classification.
Among molecular approaches, analysis of the 16S ribosomal RNA gene has become a cornerstone of

taxonomic classification.
Among molecular approaches, analysis of the 16S ribosomal RNA gene has become a cornerstone of
bacterial taxonomy because this gene contains both highly conserved and variable regions. The conserved
regions permit broad comparisons across bacterial groups, while the variable regions facilitate
differentiation among closely related species.
Whole-genome sequencing now represents the highest level of bacterial identification and
characterization, providing comprehensive information regarding taxonomy, virulence, antimicrobial
resistance, and evolutionary history.

7. Chlamydiota
Members of the phylum Chlamydiota are unique because they are obligate intracellular parasites that
cannot reproduce outside living host cells. They possess a biphasic developmental cycle consisting of
infectious elementary bodies and metabolically active reticulate bodies. Chlamydia trachomatis is
responsible for the most common bacterial sexually transmitted infection worldwide and also causes
trachoma, the leading infectious cause of preventable blindness. Chlamydia pneumoniae causes atypical
pneumonia and other respiratory tract infections. Their dependence on host cells makes laboratory
cultivation difficult, often requiring tissue culture techniques.

8. Deinococcus–Thermus
The phylum Deinococcus–Thermus contains some of the most resilient bacteria known. Members exhibit
extraordinary resistance to ionizing radiation, ultraviolet light, dehydration, and oxidative stress.

source of Taq DNA polymerase, the thermostable enzyme that revolutionized molecular biology through
the development of the Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR).

Fusobacteria are Gram-negative, anaerobic rods commonly found in the human oral cavity,
gastrointestinal tract, and female reproductive system. They participate in the formation of dental plaque

nucleatum has received considerable attention because of its association with colorectal cancer, adverse

Historically, fungi were originally classified as plants because they possess cell walls and are generally non-

known as the Kingdom Fungi.

are prokaryotic, fungal cells possess a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane. They also contain
membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes,
and vacuoles.
The presence of these organelles allows for compartmentalization of cellular activities, resulting in greater
structural and functional complexity. The fungal genome is organized into multiple linear chromosomes
located within the nucleus, and cellular respiration occurs within mitochondria. Because fungi are

The body of most fungi consists of microscopic thread-like structures known as hyphae. Hyphae grow by
elongation at their tips and collectively form an interconnected network called the mycelium. The
mycelium constitutes the vegetative portion of the fungus and is responsible for nutrient absorption and
growth. Extensive branching of hyphae increases the surface area available for nutrient uptake, enabling
fungi to exploit substrates efficiently.
Hyphae may be classified as septate or aseptate. Septate hyphae possess cross walls known as septa that
divide the hypha into compartments. Examples include species of Aspergillus, Penicillium, and Fusarium.

Spore production is a defining characteristic of fungi. Spores serve as reproductive units, dispersal

Fungi play essential ecological roles as decomposers of organic matter. By breaking down cellulose, lignin,

biochemical, immunological, and molecular characteristics. Accurate identification is essential in

Serological techniques utilize antigen-antibody reactions to detect fungal components or host immune
responses. These methods are especially valuable for diagnosing systemic fungal infections where culture
may be difficult or time-consuming.

Modern fungal identification increasingly relies on molecular techniques due to their high sensitivity and
specificity. Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR), DNA sequencing, Restriction Fragment Length

diagnosis. Analysis of ribosomal DNA regions, particularly the Internal Transcribed Spacer (ITS) region, is
widely regarded as the molecular standard for fungal identification. These techniques permit rapid and
accurate identification of fungi, including species that are difficult or impossible to culture.

them control what they do every day. One of these activities is called excretion. Inside the cells
of living things, a process called metabolism happens. This process produces both helpful and
harmful substances. If harmful substances build up, they can hurt the living thing. So, living
things get rid of these waste products from their bodies, and this is called excretion. Different
living things get rid of waste in different ways. This lecture will look at how plants get rid of
waste and how it’s different from animals.

Chemical reactions occur in the cells of living organisms all the time to carry out the life
processes. The sum of these reactions is called metabolism. Metabolism produces useful
products as well as toxic (poisonous) by-products. These toxic substances have to be removed as
they are harmful if allowed to accumulate. The removal of metabolic waste products from the
body of an organism is known as excretion.
The major excretory products are carbon dioxide, excess water, and nitrogenous compounds like
ammonia, urea, uric acid, etc. Carbon dioxide and water are produced in the process of tissue

Excretion in human beings
Although the kidneys are the main organs of excretion, the skin, lungs and liver also help in
excretion.
Skin: Our skin has sweat glands, through which we excrete small amounts of water, urea and
salts.
Liver: The liver excretes bile, which contains bile pigments. These are produced by the
breakdown of old RBCs in the liver. As hemoglobin breaks down, its iron is retained, while the
pigment (haem) is excreted with the bile. The liver also excretes cholesterol.
Lungs: The lungs help in getting rid of carbon dioxide, formed as a result of cellular respiration,
through exhalation.

Kidney: Our excretory system consists of kidneys, blood vessels that join them, ureters, urinary
bladder and urethra. They help produce and excrete urine.
There are two bean-shaped kidneys that lie in the abdominal cavity, one on either side of the
vertebral column. The kidneys are reddish brown. Each of them is about 10 cm long and weighs
about 150 g. Although they weigh less, they receive a lot of blood for filtration.
A volume of blood nearly equivalent to that in the whole body passes through the kidneys every
four or five minutes. The kidneys produce urine to filter out the waste products, like urea and
uric acid, from the blood.

6. Adaptation to Excessive Cold (Cold Hardening)
Animals have also developed adaptations to extreme cold conditions.
Animals of colder areas possess thick fur and sub-cutaneous fat, they help in the conservation of heat.
During excessive cold, they may undergo hibernation. However, sea animals can not undergo hibernation.
Sessile animals cannot migrate. Certain sessile animals, such as barnacles and mollusks which live in very cold intertidal zones or northern shores,
several insects and spiders resist the effect of cold by a process, known as cold hardening. Such animals are called freeze-tolerant animals. They
possess ice-nucleating proteins, which induce ice formation in the extracellular spaces at very low sub-zero temperatures.

Mode of Nutrition in Plants and Animals
Mode of Nutrition in Plants
Plants primarily rely on autotrophic nutrition, specifically photoautotrophy. They use sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to synthesize their own
food through photosynthesis.
However, a few specialized plants exhibit heterotrophic or mixotrophic modes to supplement their energy needs.

However, a few specialized plants exhibit heterotrophic or mixotrophic modes to supplement their energy needs.
1. Photoautotrophy (Primary Mode) The vast majority of plants are photoautotrophs.Mechanism: They use chlorophyll to capture light energy,
converting it into chemical energy (sugars) via photosynthesis.Requirements: Sunlight, water, carbon dioxide, and essential soil minerals.

2. Heterotrophy (Specialized Exceptions) Some plants have lost their chlorophyll and rely on other organisms for nutrients.
Parasitic Plants: Extract nutrients directly from host plants using specialized roots called haustoria (e.g., Rafflesia or Mistletoe).

ts: Extract nutrients directly from host plants using specialized roots called haustoria (e.g., Rafflesia or Mistletoe).
Mycoheterotrophic Plants: Do not photosynthesize; instead, they tap into mycorrhizal fungi to steal nutrients from photosynthetic trees (e.g.,
Indian Pipe).
3. Mixotrophy (Carnivorous Plants) Certain plants are autotrophic but supplement their diet with insects to survive in nutrient-poor
soils.Mechanism: They perform photosynthesis but use modified leaves to trap and digest prey, absorbing vital nitrogen and phosphorus (e.g.,
Venus Flytrap, Pitcher Plants).

Animals rely on the heterotrophic mode of nutrition, meaning they cannot synthesize their own food and must depend on other organisms for

Minute life-forms, such as protozoans, exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide across their entire
surfaces. Multicellular organisms, in which diffusion distances are longer, generally resort to other
strategies. Aquatic worms, for example, lengthen and flatten their bodies to refresh the external

jellyfish, which can be quite large, has a low oxygen need because its content of organic matter is less
than 1 percent and its metabolizing cells are located just beneath the surface, so that diffusing
distances are small.

FLOWERING PLANTS
Flowering plants make up the largest and most diverse group of plants on Earth. They have
colonized the majority of the planet, including the oceans and sea floors. As a result, these
flowering plants, which are referred to as "angiosperms," are very important to human life. Not
only are they responsible for producing a significant portion of the oxygen that we breathe, but
they also produce fruit, vegetables, herbs, and seeds. They contribute to the ecology by
