through conflict resolution and maintenance of global peace and security. Through tools/mechanisms such as peacekeeping,
international organizations at sub-regional, regional and global levels (UN, AU, ECOWAS respectively) have increasingly
become greater agents of conflict resolution.
4.1 The United Nations: Key Organs and Mechanisms for Conflict Resolution
The UN's establishment hinges on managing and resolving conflicts to maintain international peace and security. The UN
Charter's preamble states: “We the people of United Nations determined to save succeeding generation from the scourge of
war… do hereby established an international organization to be known as United Nations (UN)” (The Charter of UN, 1945).

The UN's first purpose is to maintain international peace and security, which has conflict resolution as a basic pillar.

Peace Operations, DPO):

• Sanctions

4.1.3 Conflict Prevention and Mediation
Applies structural and diplomatic measures to keep intrastate or interstate tensions and disputes from escalating into violent
conflict. Its main tool is preventive diplomacy — diplomatic action taken to prevent disputes from escalating into conflicts
and to limit the spread of conflicts when they occur (dppa.un.org). It also entails peacemaking: early-warning systems and
mediation before, during and after conflicts. Delivered through Peace Envoys, Good Offices of the UN Secretary-General,
and political missions directed by DPPA and its Mediation Support Unit (MSU). The UN favours prevention/avoidance above
any other conflict resolution mechanism.

and its Mediation Support Unit (MSU). The UN favours prevention/avoidance above
any other conflict resolution mechanism.
4.1.4 Political Missions
Besides peacekeeping missions, the UN also operates Special Political Missions (SPMs) — special civilian missions
engaged in conflict prevention and resolution of emerging deadly conflicts, and sustenance of peace through post-conflict
peacebuilding worldwide. They provide prompt responses with assistance in mediations and reconciliations, facilitation of
peace agreements, elections, rule of law, and monitoring human-rights violations (Better World Campaign, 2022). SPMs
include country-specific missions, panels and regional offices, Good Offices of the UN Secretary-General, and
Personal/Special Envoys of the UNSG.

Personal/Special Envoys of the UNSG. Current SPMs are more than double the number of existing UN peacekeeping
operations, and are supported by DPPA.
4.1.5 Peacemaking
A reconciliatory, diplomatic tool used to address an ongoing or emerging conflict, especially by facilitating a negotiated
agreement between warring parties (UN DPKO/DFS, 2008). It occurs under peacekeeping, peacebuilding, and other
occasions; DPPA and DPO are actively involved. Example: in the 2015 Malian conflict, a UN peacekeeping mission
facilitated a peace agreement between the Malian state and armed groups.

4.1.6 Peacebuilding
Mostly diplomatic, political and developmental activities used to sustain peace and avert a relapse into conflict in a
post-conflict state — strengthening national capacities for conflict management and laying the foundation for sustainable
peace and development (UN DPKO, 2008). Includes electoral assistance, promotion of justice, removal of root causes of
conflict, reconstruction, and humanitarian assistance. Numerous organisations are involved, including the World Bank, IMF,
DPPA and the Peacebuilding Commission.
4.1.7 Sanctions
A coercive instrument in which the UN Security Council imposes an embargo on an aggressive state or group to facilitate
compliance.

instrument in which the UN Security Council imposes an embargo on an aggressive state or group to facilitate
compliance. Though coercive, it is not violent and falls short of peace enforcement (which UN peace operations largely
avoid); enforcement is usually left to a coalition of willing states or regional organizations after Security Council authorization.
Examples:
• 2011: intervention in Libya authorized by UNSC Resolution 1973 (2011), implemented by NATO.

8. Challenges Faced by International Organizations (UN, AU, ECOWAS)
8.1 Logistics and Financial Constraints
The scale and complexity of modern multidimensional peace support missions require heavy budgets and high-level logistics
that UN member states and allied regional organizations struggle to meet, constraining timely deployment and mission
completion.
8.2 Complexity of Conflicts and Conflict Resolution
Some conflicts combine violence from rebels, extremists, terrorists and trans-border criminal groups (e.g. Mali, Somalia,
Congo, Sudan), presenting great difficulty for UN and especially ECOWAS conflict management, and leading to high fatality
rates among peacekeepers.

reat difficulty for UN and especially ECOWAS conflict management, and leading to high fatality
rates among peacekeepers.
8.3 External and Special Interests Pursued by Great Powers
Member-state policies can oppose collective will. Terrif and Keeley (2007) argue that high expectations of UN
conflict-management ability have been reduced/influenced by member states' interests, especially major powers. Example:
France's undue influence over the MINUSMA stabilization mission in Mali — France eventually exited Mali after the recent
military takeover.
8.4 Inadequate Institutional Structure
The huge size and complex decision-making/administrative structure of organizations like the UN and AU make rapid

deployment difficult, since the UN lacks its own stand-by force and depends on Troop Contributing Countries (TCCs).
8.5 Deficient Cooperation in UN–Regional Organizations' Peace Operations
Example: in the Malian conflict (2011–2013), UN–AU/ECOWAS collaboration was strained, especially during the transition
from the African-Led International Support Mission to Mali (AFISMA) to the UN Multidimensional Integrated Stabilisation
Mission in Mali (MINUSMA). Financial/logistics incapacity and external interest have sometimes hindered regional
organizations' cooperation in UN-led missions even within their own regions.

9. Summary and Conclusion
International organizations continue to actively manage and resolve conflicts worldwide, particularly in Africa, helping save
future generations from the scourge of war. Peacekeeping is the most prominent/active UN tool; preventive diplomacy and
mediation are the most preferred mechanism. Challenges span administrative, financial, structural, capacity/logistic and
doctrinal areas. UN Secretary-General António Guterres is restructuring the UN peace architecture (reforms in DPPA and
DPO; the A4P — Action for Peacekeeping — initiative) toward a more people-centred approach with special concern for
human rights protection.

the continent.

The Media: An Overview
Media is broadly a channel of communication — a powerful tool for communicating ideas and sharing information, news,
entertainment and messages with large groups of people, cutting across regions and boundaries (Ayodele, 2022). Freedom
of expression is not only the core of a healthy media but a fundamental human right, vital for a democratic structure (Kuusik,
2010).

is not only the core of a healthy media but a fundamental human right, vital for a democratic structure (Kuusik,
2010). As the “fourth estate,” media is susceptible to manipulation positively and otherwise regardless of the issue of
discourse (Abubakar, 2021), and it contributes to peace building through non-partisan, balanced information, accountability,
and direct conflict-related programmes (Spurk, 2002).
The Role of the Media in Society
• Information Dissemination: media serve as gatekeepers, reporting events, political developments, scientific
discoveries and social issues so people can be informed (Murugesan, 2023; Okoro, Icha-Ituma & Okunna, 2020).

within the locality (Nwosu, 2022) — systems of governance and social structures rooted in established customs, traditions
and cultural practices, described as key in promoting peace building in every society (Lamai, 2020). Examples: traditional

rulers, elders, traditional courts, customary practices, age grades and religious institutions.

What is Peace Building?
The implementation of measures intended to create or sustain peace, especially in an area affected by conflict. The Kroc
Institute for International Peace Studies (2025) describes it as the development of constructive personal, group and political

ute for International Peace Studies (2025) describes it as the development of constructive personal, group and political
relationships across ethnic, religious, national and racial boundaries, aiming to resolve injustice non-violently and transform
the structural conditions that generate deadly conflict; it includes conflict prevention, management, resolution/transformation
and post-conflict reconciliation. Christofis (2020) similarly describes peace building as a complex process involving multiple
actors and requiring values, goals and commitment to human rights and needs — aiming to establish durable peace and

The Media and Peace Building
Media's role in peace building cuts two ways: it can report and reflect on pressing issues, or it can be used for propaganda
and to cover things up, curtailing people's freedom and right to information. Countering disinformation involves strategies to
address the spread of false or misleading information, primarily to protect public trust and prevent harm (Kuusik, 2010): lack
of information can make people desperate, restless and easy to manipulate. Impartial, independent global media is essential
for informing the global community and supporting those directly impacted, but since only a limited number of conflicts

for informing the global community and supporting those directly impacted, but since only a limited number of conflicts
receive international coverage, local media's role is particularly crucial. During the #EndSARS protests against Nigerian
police brutality, the media informed the masses of the factual story behind the protest, countering misconceptions between
youths and the police (Ogbemi, 2020).
Fundamental roles of media in peacebuilding:
• Information Provider: non-partisan, balanced, accurate information and accountability (Spurk, 2002); creates
awareness of trending/emerging development issues.

Countering Disinformation in Peace Building
Disinformation is more than the spread of false information — it is structural and systemic, often produced with intent to harm
and then shared more widely by people who may not intend to deceive at all (Marx, 2025). Per Connors & Baumhofer
(2025), peace-building approaches align with strengthening democratic institutions; media can lead storytelling campaigns,
host trust-building dialogues with conflict actors, and address the impact of social-media disinformation (Okocha, Akpe &
Odeba, 2024). The media counters disinformation through:

3.0 Main Content
The late 20th/early 21st centuries saw the evolution of international humanitarian law, emphasizing protection of civilians and
accountability for war crimes; the International Criminal Court (ICC), established 2002, aims to address impunity for atrocities
in post-conflict societies (IDMC, 2021). Today, post-conflict situations are often protracted crises where recovery is hindered
by ongoing violence, political instability and humanitarian needs — exemplified by the Syrian Civil War and the conflicts in

South Sudan and Yemen, which require navigating both immediate needs and long-term rebuilding (UN-OCHA, 2021).
Features of Post-Conflict Situations
• Humanitarian Crises: widespread displacement (IDMC, 2021) creates a dual crisis — refugees needing assistance
across international borders, and IDPs remaining within their home countries.
• Economic Instability: armed conflict disrupts local economies, destroying infrastructure, ending livelihoods and raising
poverty; countries emerging from conflict face high unemployment and inflation (World Bank, 2020).

The Refugee Crisis
Article 1 of the 1951 Convention defines a refugee as someone who, owing to a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons
of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion, is outside their country of nationality
and unable or unwilling to avail themselves of its protection (or, being stateless, is outside their former habitual residence
and unable/unwilling to return) (UNHCR, 2001–2002).
Causes of the Refugee Crisis:
• Armed Conflict: prolonged violence/warfare directly displaces populations; civilians are often targeted, prompting flight
(UNHCR, 2022).

prolonged violence/warfare directly displaces populations; civilians are often targeted, prompting flight
(UNHCR, 2022).
• Persecution: systematic persecution based on ethnicity, religion, or political beliefs — manifesting as violence,
discrimination and human-rights abuses (Smith, 2021).
• Natural Disasters: conflict can exacerbate natural-disaster impacts, increasing displacement and stress on resources
(IDMC, 2021).
Challenges faced by refugees: access to basic services (healthcare, education, shelter — Benson & O'Neill, 2020), legal
protection (complex/bureaucratic asylum procedures — UNHCR, 2022), and psychosocial support for displacement-related
trauma (Morris, 2022). Host nations may experience resource strain and tensions with local populations; the international

rauma (Morris, 2022). Host nations may experience resource strain and tensions with local populations; the international

Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs)
IDPs are individuals/groups forced to flee their homes or habitual residence, particularly as a result of or to avoid the effects
of armed conflict, generalized violence, human-rights violations, or natural/human-made disasters, who have not crossed an
internationally recognized state border (UNHCR, 2022).

Role of UN-OCHA in Managing Post-Conflict Situations
UN-OCHA coordinates international humanitarian efforts among governments, NGOs and local communities, serving as a
central hub for information-sharing and strategic planning to avoid duplication of effort. It leads resource mobilization/funding

ub for information-sharing and strategic planning to avoid duplication of effort. It leads resource mobilization/funding

Community leaders are crucial intermediaries between affected populations and humanitarian actors. They facilitate

Challenges in Managing Post-Conflict Situations
• Security Instability: ongoing violence, unrest or armed groups restrict humanitarian access and deter displaced people
from returning home (Khan, 2020).
• Lack of Funding and Resources: heavy reliance on external donor funding, which is often insufficient — forcing
organizations to prioritize some needs over others (Benson & O'Neill, 2020).
• Fragmentation of Humanitarian Efforts: numerous actors (NGOs, local organizations, international agencies) can

2020).
• Fragmentation of Humanitarian Efforts: numerous actors (NGOs, local organizations, international agencies) can
create overlaps, gaps and inefficiencies without strong coordination (UN-OCHA, 2021).
• Cultural and Social Barriers: deep social divisions and mistrust among groups hinder collaborative efforts and social
cohesion (Fischer, 2019).
• Psychosocial Impact of Conflict: trauma, grief and mental-health issues impede recovery engagement; adequate
support services are often lacking (Morris, 2022).
• Political Obstacles: political instability or government resistance can impede humanitarian programmes; political
agendas may distribute resources inequitably, and bureaucratic hurdles delay aid and limit local-actor participation
(Smith, 2021).

Managing post-conflict situations requires coordinated efforts among international organizations, NGOs, community leaders
and local populations to address refugee/IDP needs, restore infrastructure, and rebuild social cohesion. UN-OCHA ensures
coordinated, resourced humanitarian response; NGOs deliver immediate assistance and long-term support while building
local capacity; community leaders enhance recovery through communication, conflict resolution and resource mobilization.
